narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold used by the admissions process, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average accepted student ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the bottom decile. This low ranking was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance and worked in your favor. At 3.00 it sits slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw this performance as a modest positive signal for eventual bar success. Your LSAT score of 28, however, pulled the prediction back toward failure. It is substantially lower than the 37-point average among accepted applicants and therefore increased the model’s concern about your readiness.

Taken together, the weak third-year ranking and low LSAT outweighed the encouraging aspects of your record, producing the 65% failure probability that led to rejection.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a significantly higher score, combined with any opportunity to demonstrate improved academic performance, would most directly address the concerns that caused this decision.
